title: A Songbook for the Kitchen
premise: Gideon Zhou has spent eleven years raising her daughter alone in the small town of Marrow Creek, running the bookshop she inherited and telling herself the silence around her daughter's other parent is a kindness. When a water-damaged letter postmarked 2014 falls out of a donated cookbook, it reveals that the person who left — her old best friend and first love, Wren Halloway — never meant to disappear; the letter was intercepted by Gideon's late grandmother, who wanted to protect the shop, and Gideon, from a life she thought was ruin. As the autumn festival approaches, Wren returns as the festival's hired organizer, forcing both women to reckon with stolen years, the town's comfortable lies, and Gideon's own complicity in choosing safety over truth. Forgiving Wren proves easier than forgiving herself, but on the last night of the festival, Gideon chooses honesty over the mirror's old verdict — and they begin again, slowly, with the letter finally read aloud.
about_author: Kestrel Villalobos is a former line cook turned bookseller who writes love stories set in kitchens, shops, and towns that keep secrets. She lives in the Pacific Northwest with her partner, two cats, and an ever-growing collection of annotated cookbooks.

chapters.title: Water Damage
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. While boxing donations for the autumn book sale, Gideon finds a swollen letter tucked inside a donated cookbook — addressed to her, postmarked eleven years ago. Her hands shake as she recognizes Wren's handwriting but can't bring herself to open it. The beat is dread disguised as routine: the past arriving in an ordinary afternoon.

chapters.title: The Unopened Year
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, with flashbacks to 2014. She locks the letter in the register drawer and tries to run the shop, but memories surface: the fight, the packed car, the promise she made never to chase anyone again. Her teenage daughter, Juniper, notices something's wrong. The emotional beat is avoidance — grief rehearsed so long it looks like calm.

chapters.title: Festival Contracts
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren arrives in Marrow Creek as the festival's contracted organizer, telling herself this is strictly business. She learns Gideon still runs the bookshop and nearly drives back out of town that night. The beat is fear wearing professionalism: she came for closure and found a living wound instead.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Sorting her late grandmother's papers for probate, Gideon finds drafts of letters to Wren and a bank record showing the grandmother quietly bought out Wren's family debt the week she left. The letter wasn't lost — it was hidden. The beat is betrayal reframing everything: the villain may have been the woman who raised her.

chapters.title: Flour and Accusation
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Festival planning forces Gideon and Wren into the same kitchen for the fundraiser bake. Between measuring cups they trade barbs that are really questions: Why didn't you come back? Why didn't you look? Neither answers honestly. The beat is friction as intimacy — anger burning hotter than either expected.

chapters.title: Juniper's Question
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Juniper, who has pieced together who Wren is, confronts her mother: 'You decided for me before I was born.' Gideon defends her choices and hears, in her own voice, her grandmother's logic. The beat is the theme sharpened — protection and control are the same act seen from different sides of a door.

chapters.title: The Letter, Read
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Unable to sleep, Wren writes a new letter she'll never send, then finally asks Gideon directly whether the old one ever arrived. Gideon, cornered, admits it did — and that she never opened it. The beat is devastation: eleven years of blame collapse into the discovery that Wren never stopped reaching.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Weather
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. They read the letter together in the closed bookshop at midnight — Wren's account of the debt, the shame, the plan to return by spring. Old fury gives way to shared mourning. The beat is tenderness after rupture, shadowed by a harder question neither can dodge: what did each of them choose, when no one forced them?

chapters.title: The Person in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, climax eve. On the festival's opening day, Gideon confronts her own role: she let the letter stay sealed because hope was more dangerous than certainty. She apologizes to Juniper without excuses, then to Wren publicly, at the bake table, in front of the whole town. The beat is the cost of survival named aloud — and paid.

chapters.title: Last Night of the Festival
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, resolution. Under the lanterns, Wren offers no grand gesture — only a question about staying, asked slowly, with room to refuse. Gideon says yes to a beginning, not a rescue: dinners, honest letters, Juniper setting terms. The final image is the letter framed above the kitchen table where they cook together. The beat is belonging earned, not granted.
